claims.text: Conventional processing of high-entropy alloys typically produces a relatively homogeneous microstructure.
Controlled thermo-mechanical temperature and deformation cycles can induce a duplex/lamellar microstructure.
Controlled thermo-mechanical processing can stabilize the induced duplex/lamellar microstructure.
The processing will be effective when alloy composition and phase stability permit controlled phase separation.
The processing benefit will diminish in alloys that resist duplex or lamellar formation.
Excessive thermo-mechanical processing can cause coarsening or unwanted phase transformations.
Alternating phases in a duplex/lamellar microstructure distribute stress.
Alternating phases enhance dislocation motion.
A dual-phase structure improves load distribution and activates multiple toughening mechanisms.
The duplex/lamellar structure promotes crack bridging and crack deflection.
The proposed microstructural mechanisms improve the balance between strength and ductility.
Structural stability from the duplex/lamellar configuration can improve Young's modulus.
Crack bridging and deflection improve fracture resistance.
The processed alloy will show a statistically significant increase in tensile strength relative to conventionally processed alloys.
The processed alloy will show a statistically significant increase in ductility relative to conventionally processed alloys.
The processed alloy will show a statistically significant increase in fracture toughness relative to conventionally processed alloys.
Young's modulus will be maintained or slightly increased by the processing.
Thermodynamically unfavorable phase separation prevents the hypothesis from holding.
Slow or otherwise limiting diffusion kinetics can prevent formation of a stable duplex/lamellar structure.
Excessive grain growth or deleterious phase transformations can negate the proposed mechanical-property benefits.
